analysis.investment_thesis: EMIL fails both legs of the Magic Formula — earnings yield of ~7.5% (EBIT INR 451 Cr / EV ~INR 5,991 Cr) is well below my 12% threshold, and ROIC of ~13% (EBIT / capital employed of ~INR 3,533 Cr) is below my 20% minimum. This is a low-margin retailer that consumes rather than generates capital.
key_strengths: Revenue growing at 17% CAGR (2020-2025), demonstrating real store expansion traction in underpenetrated South India
High promoter holding of 65.17% aligns management with shareholders
Strong brand recognition across 6 retail formats with 40+ year operating history
key_risks: FCF has been negative 3 of last 3 years (-INR 247 Cr, -14 Cr, -159 Cr) — the business destroys cash as it grows
Borrowings surged from INR 872 Cr (2020) to INR 1,963 Cr (2025), with finance costs eating into thin 4% operating margins
Net profit fell from INR 184 Cr to INR 160 Cr in FY2025 despite revenue growing — operating leverage is absent in this model
red_flags: Earnings yield of ~7.5% is well below my 12% floor — paying too much for a mediocre business
ROIC ~12-13% (ROCE stated 10.4%) — specialty retail with no pricing power earns returns near its cost of capital
Capex of INR 335 Cr in FY2025 against OCF of INR 176 Cr means every rupee of growth requires borrowed capital
Net profit declining YoY (FY24: 184 Cr → FY25: 160 Cr) even as revenue grew 10.8% — margin compression accelerating
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Running the Magic Formula on EMIL: EBIT is INR 451 Cr (FY2025); Enterprise Value = market cap INR 4,046 Cr + net debt INR 1,945 Cr ≈ INR 5,991 Cr. Earnings yield = 7.5% — below my 12% hurdle. Capital employed (equity + debt) is ~INR 3,533 Cr, giving ROIC of ~12.8%, consistent with the stated ROCE of 10.4%. Neither metric clears my thresholds, and a business that earns returns near its cost of capital has no moat worth paying for.

The structural problem is the consumer electronics retail model itself: 4% operating margins, thin gross margins of 14%, and a store-expansion strategy that requires perpetual debt-funded capex. The forward P/E of 23x implies a major earnings re-rating that I don't see a path to given rising finance costs (up 13.4% CAGR), negative FCF, and a debt/equity ratio of 1.26. Greenblatt's formula rewards businesses that earn high returns on tangible capital without needing much of it — EMIL is the opposite: capital-hungry, low-returning, and getting more indebted each year to sustain growth.
